From **Statement 7** (Sal): Says exactly 2 of {Alejandro=truth, Mark, Micah} tell truth. Since Alejandro is true and Mark/Micah have opposite values (exactly 1), that's 2 total. So **Sal tells the truth**.

From **Statement 20** (Shalonda): Sal tells truth, so **Shalonda tells the truth**.

From **Statement 24** (Gwenn): Says exactly 2 of {Shalonda=truth, Octavio, Osborn} tell truth. We have Shalonda true and Octavio/Osborn opposite values (exactly 1), so 2 total. So **Gwenn tells the truth**.

From **Statement 28** (Conception): Says all three or exactly one of {Gwenn=truth, Misty, Olivia} tell truth. Whether Misty/Olivia are both true (giving 3) or both false (giving 1), the statement is true. So **Conception tells the truth**.

From **Statement 1** (Raymond): The logic shows Raymond and Jamey have opposite values.

Therefore: If Raymond=true, then Jamey=false, then Conception=true ✓. If Raymond=false, then Jamey=true, then Conception=false ✗.

Since Conception is true, **Raymond must be false**.

From **Statement 9** (Alexis): Says all three or exactly one of {Ryan=false, Osian, Mustafa} tell truth. Since Ryan is false and Osian/Mustafa have same value, we have either 0 or 2 truth-tellers (both scenarios give neither "all three" nor "exactly one"). So **Alexis lies**.
